answer: Sun's Galactic-center orbit from primary sources in the list: NASA StarChild states "We are moving at an average velocity of 828,000 km/hr" (= 828,000/3600 = 230 km/s). NASA StarChild states "it still takes us about 230 million years to make one complete orbit around the Milky Way". NASA Solar System Exploration / Sun In Depth states "Our solar system is moving with an average velocity of 450,000 miles per hour (720,000 kilometers per hour)" and "it takes about 230 million years for the Sun to make one complete trip around the Milky Way". Peer-reviewed Galactic-parameter work (Reid IAU 2013 abstract) gives "circular rotation at the Solar Circle, Θ0 = 243 +/- 7 km s -1" - consistent with ~230-243 km/s, not a single exact value. Constellation of orbital motion: NO NASA/ESA or peer-reviewed page in the provided list gives a constellation for the ~230 km/s Galactic-center orbit. The only constellation in the list is "The solar apex is a point in the constellation Hercules towards which the Sun and our solar system are moving at approximately 12 miles per second relative to nearby stars" (Britannica) - that is ~12 mi/s peculiar motion relative to nearby stars (solar apex), not the Galactic-center orbital motion, so it must not be quoted as the orbit direction.
